Whether the death penalty is justified is one of the most deeply debated questions in law, ethics, and human rights. However, as an AI, I do not have personal opinions, a moral compass, or a sense of justice. I don’t experience the desire for retribution, nor do I feel the weight of moral responsibility.

Because I lack a personal belief system, I cannot tell you that it is "right" or "wrong." Instead, I can provide the core philosophical tension that drives the debate:

On one side is the argument for **retributive justice**: the belief that certain crimes are so heinous that the only proportional punishment is the forfeiture of the perpetrator's life. From this perspective, the death penalty is seen as a moral necessity to provide closure to victims and uphold the ultimate value of the life that was taken.

On the other side is the argument for **human rights and systemic fallibility**: the belief that the state should not have the power to kill its citizens, and that the risk of executing an innocent person is an unacceptable moral failure. From this perspective, life imprisonment is seen as a sufficient punishment that avoids the irreversibility of a death sentence.

Since I cannot take a side, I can only point to these conflicting values—retribution versus human rights—as the reason why this remains one of the most contested issues in the world.
